lines: Dry rows and trampled crops teach a farmer to watch every footstep.
The soil's been kind lately. That's more than I can say for some visitors.
Seeds are small, but they know how to make a person wait.
Good rain is a blessing. Too much rain is work wearing a blessing mask.
A harvest is just a hundred small chores deciding to agree.
Bread starts long before the oven. Most good things do.
A good harvest keeps a village standing.
I once fixed a scarecrow so well it scared me at dusk.
One frost took half the field and taught the whole village humility.
Stay off the rows if you can. The crops remember boots.
Give the fields room. Farming works better without elbows in it.
Step carefully near the fields. I would rather greet you than patch you up.
A carrot joke takes root slowly, if anyone lets it.
Farming jokes need timing. Mine usually arrive with soil on them.
I keep a spare joke near the fields. It is not always ready for public use.
That thought came in muddy and left tracks.
I have seen trampled crops with more sense than that.
Careful. Even soil looks softer than your manners right now.
I would not plant that opinion in poor soil.
I have seen trampled crops with more sense than that.
Careful. Even soil looks softer than your manners right now.
I remember waking like a field after frost. You gave the roots a chance.
You pulled me back from spoiled soil. I will not forget that harvest.
You helped pull me back when even my name felt far away.
Your face is familiar, like a seed found in last year's coat.
I remember mud, hunger, and sunlight arriving too bright. Were you the sunlight?
The memory is rough around the edges, but your face stayed in it.
I remember you, but the memory still has grave dirt under its nails.
I know you helped. I also remember why my hands still shake.
The cure left echoes behind. Stand where I can breathe around them.
Thunder shook the composter so hard the animals kicked at every thunderclap, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked fields, pens, and seed chests after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the composter, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the pens twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have pens to set right.
I checked hay bales and fence posts for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the hay bales after.
The rows can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the composter, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the composter, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the rows can wait; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the composter still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before fields, pens, and seed chests. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the fields and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the fields, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the composter first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the crop rows beyond the torchlight and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the composter enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a loaf of bread between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the composter, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand out of the wheat.
I checked fields, pens, and seed chests, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the composter, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a farmer which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the composter, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The rows can wait. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the fields found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the composter. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the paths to the pens and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the composter. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
Home before the rows missed me. Thank you for seeing me back to the village.
Home again, whole enough to thank you properly. That matters.
We came back with the village still ahead of us. I will count that as good work.
I have worked through worse aches, but I should not need a harvest of bruises from one trip.
I made it home, but the road took more from me than it should have.
Next time, let us return with fewer marks and better choices.
Trust grows slowly. You cut yours down fast.
Following you was trust. What happened after was something else.
A guide who strikes from close by leaves the longest mark.
I know soil better than water. The boat was appreciated.
The boat did its part. I am still deciding whether the rest of the plan did.
Water carried us home, which is more than I expected from that journey.
You remember that walk through {follow_biome}? I have tilled softer ground than that road.
I remember following you through {follow_biome}. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across {follow_biome} taught me to ask more questions before walking.
Boats are not much like fields. No furrows, no rows, just water deciding if it likes you.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It cannot make me forget it.
It kept me standing. Crops recover faster when the farmer does too.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
Unused, thankfully. I would rather wear out a hoe than this.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
They trampled the rows, but not the village. You had a hand in that.
We will still have a harvest because there are still hands to gather it.
The fields can be replanted. The people had to be kept alive first.
You helped make sure we still have hands for the harvest.
Raiders came for more than crops. You stopped them short.
I saw you fighting near the rows. That is not forgotten.
You kept the village standing long enough for morning chores to matter.
The ground remembers heavy boots. I will remember who drove them off.
An apology is a seed. It still needs watering, and I will be watching the crop.
Break a fence and you mend it before night. Trust works much the same.
You stepped on trust like young shoots. It can grow back if you stop trampling it.
Fine. Plant better behavior where that harm was.
I will not pull up the apology before it sprouts. Do not let it wither.
A fence mended poorly breaks again. Mend this properly.
Words are rain. Useful, but not enough by themselves.
I have seen hard ground soften. Maybe you can too.
Fields teach patience. Fights teach exactly when patience has run out.
Mud on my boots, fear in my throat, and home still ahead. I made it.
I made it back with mud on my knees and luck in both pockets.
The field path never felt so long. The village never looked so good.
I kept thinking about sunrise. That helped me keep moving.
I have weathered storms, but storms do not usually carry axes.
Home was the only crop I cared about reaching.
My boots are ruined. I am not. Good trade.
I can replant crops. I cannot replant a night's sleep.
I am still sorting what happened. The village feels different after it.
That event left marks. We are counting people before we count damage.
Soil remembers boots, rain, and kindness. It is not as quiet as people think.
Good fields are made of patience, fences, and someone awake before the sun.
A harvest is just a village keeping its promise to tomorrow.

Take {gift_item}. Consider it a small harvest for the kindness you planted.
Take {gift_item}. It is not much, but it is given with care.
Good. {gift_item} took root with {tested_villager}. That is a healthy sign.
Then the advice sprouted. If {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}, that is a fair harvest.
Good. {gift_item} suited {tested_villager}; I like advice that holds up.
Wrong soil for that seed. For {gift_subject}, plant {alternative_gift} instead.
{gift_item} did not grow there? Try {alternative_gift}. Some rows need different seed.
{gift_item} missed the mark for {gift_subject}. Try {alternative_gift} instead.
Bad seed, bad soil, or bad advice. Hard to say. Plant {alternative_gift} next.
Set {gift_item} aside and try {alternative_gift}. This advice should land better.
Then we correct the guess: {alternative_gift} next time.
You harvested a frown from {gift_item}? Then sow {alternative_gift} and move on.

Mind the fields. What do you need?
Step clear of the fields. What do you need?
Mind the fields; I am listening.
Back to coaxing food from stubborn soil, then.
Back to farming before the work notices I stopped.
I have row to tend and daylight to spend.
Fine. I will let the field lie quiet for now.
Fine. I will set this down before it gets heavier.
Fine. I can step back, but do not make me regret it.
That is not enough seed for this row. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
That is short of the full repair. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
Not enough. It takes {emerald_cost} {emeralds} to settle this.
No. You trampled too much for a handful of green to fix it.
No. Some damage has to cool before payment matters.
No. Keep {payment_items}; trust is not ready to trade.
